L11@P2: FOREWORD
L12@P2: The goal of this publication is to briefly describe the common threats and
L13@P2: opportunities that the US and the Netherlands share in the areas of integrated
L14@P2: water management, flood protection, disaster response and climate change.
L15@P2: Hurricane Katrina reminded officials in both countries that absolute safety
L16@P2: is not possible, and that a robust, multi-disciplinary approach to integrated
L17@P2: water management and climate change is necessary. Living with water presents
L18@P2: numerous challenges and incredible opportunities. With this booklet we hope
L19@P2: to stimulate the reader to imagine how the Netherlands and the U.S.—two
L20@P2: of the world’s oldest friends, key allies and important trading partners—can
L21@P2: further deepen their relationship and jointly solve key engineering, scientific
L22@P2: and public policy questions.
L23@P2: The contents of the booklet were derived from various sources of public information. Any fault with the contents is attributable solely to the Embassy. No
L24@P2: rights or obligations, explicit or implied, are afforded by or can be taken from
L25@P2: this publication.

L48@P4: vigilant. While we inspect every meter of every dike, levee, gate, barrier, and
L49@P4: sluice in the Netherlands, we understand that a zero percent risk of failure
L50@P4: is an unattainable goal. We also know that imagination, innovation, constant
L51@P4: maintenance, new technology, better risk assessment tools, and preparing
L52@P4: for “what if” scenarios are crucial to our national survival.
L53@P4: Hurricane Katrina’s devastation shocked and saddened the world. The Dutch
L54@P4: were reminded of their own terrible flood in 1953 and the U.S. government’s
L55@P4: prompt dispatch of helicopters and aid. To help our friends in Louisiana and
L56@P4: Mississippi, my government immediately dispatched mobile pumps, naval ships,
L57@P4: food, medicine, and other supplies to the U.S. Gulf Coast. Since then, the Dutch
L58@P4: have discussed with U.S. public and private sector officials how Dutch expertise
L59@P4: and technology might strengthen U.S. hurricane and flood protection systems.
L60@P4: Policymakers from California, Florida, New York and the Netherlands are sharing
L61@P4: best practices on water system management, climate change, environmental
L62@P4: restoration, disaster and emergency response, and sound waterfront development.
L63@P4: Deep and lasting partnerships—government-to-government, university-to-university,
L64@P4: business-to-business—and two-way, multi-disciplinary interaction are key.
L65@P4: The Netherlands was the first foreign country to salute the U.S. flag in 1776, and
L66@P4: we have joined together many times since to confront common threats. Effective
L67@P4: water management is not a new challenge, but as the world’s climate changes
L68@P4: and brings with it new problems and opportunities, close Dutch-American cooperation can yield economic efficiencies and safety benefits of great magnitude.
L69@P4: This small booklet provides a brief overview of this very fruitful and growing
L70@P4: cooperation. I welcome you to contact our Embassy or any of the Dutch organizations mentioned herein for more information or guidance.
L71@P4: Crown Prince Willem Alexander of the Netherlands
L72@P4: INTRODUCTION
L73@P4: Water is a crucial feature of the American landscape. Development and expansion
L74@P4: on and near the Mighty Mississippi, the Hudson, the Missouri, the Ohio, the
L75@P4: Kissimmee rivers are milepost markers on the roadmap of American progress.
L76@P4: New York, New Orleans, San Francisco, Chicago, Boston, Seattle, St. Louis and
L77@P4: Miami are great cities because of their proximity to water.
L78@P4: Across the United States, public awareness of effective water management is
L79@P4: growing. Hurricanes, floods, droughts, and water shortages, contamination,
L80@P4: storage, and conveyance create unique challenges for American policymakers.
L81@P4: One of America’s oldest friends—the Netherlands—is also confronting these
L82@P4: same challenges.
L83@P4: The Netherlands’ struggle with water has defined its history. Water has been
L84@P4: friend and foe alike—a source of vitality and a source of devastation. Democratic
L85@P4: government first appeared in about 1300 AD when Dutch merchants and farmers
L86@P4: created local water boards to “keep people’s feet dry.” Eight hundred years later,
L87@P4: Dutch water boards, in partnership with local and national government, have turned
L88@P4: coastal swamps, huge inland lakes, and low-lying bogs into productive land used
L89@P4: for farming, recreation, flood control, urban growth, commerce, housing, and more.
L90@P4: “While God Created the Earth, the Dutch created the Netherlands” is an old Dutch
L91@P4: saying. Two-thirds of the country is at or below sea level, subject to river flooding
L92@P4: and tidal inundation. Yet more than 11 million people—two-thirds of all Dutch
L93@P4: citizens—live in, and 70 percent of Dutch gross-domestic product is produced
L94@P4: in, these flood-prone areas. Our world-class water management practices and
L95@P4: innovative flood protection infrastructure represent a multifaceted, integrated,
L96@P4: and constantly evolving response to many near and real disasters. We like living
L97@P4: with the water—it is a source of great prosperity—but we know we must remain

L125@P6: THE NETHERLANDS’
L126@P6: EXPERIENCE
L127@P6: Flood Control
L128@P6: The topography of the Netherlands has made the Dutch world-class experts in
L129@P6: the planning, design, construction, and maintenance of dams, levees, surge
L130@P6: barriers, and other flood control structures. Through research and experience,
L131@P6: the Dutch have acquired specialized knowledge in levee failure mechanisms
L132@P6: (piping, seepage, overtopping, unequal pressures, etc.); have designed unique
L133@P6: software and assessment techniques to predict potential levee failure; and
L134@P6: have developed innovative techniques—mixed in place, expanding columns,
L135@P6: nails in levees, automated counterbalance—to strengthen weakened urban
L136@P6: levees. Moreover, the Netherlands is unique in the world for its use of ‘soft’
L137@P6: measures to enhance wetlands and prevent erosion along its coast.
L138@P6: The Delta Works
L139@P6: The Netherlands’ Delta Works is the world’s largest flood protection project.
L140@P6: Begun after the devastating 1953 floods in the province of Zeeland in the
L141@P6: southwestern Netherlands, the Delta Works include:
L142@P6: • the Eastern Scheldt Barrier, a five-mile long storm surge barrier along the
L143@P6: North Sea coast that rests in the open position to preserve the unique
L144@P6: ecology of the estuary
L145@P6: • 1800 miles of primary levees and 8500 miles of secondary levees
L146@P6: • more than 300 secondary dams—some quite large—gates and sluices that
L147@P6: have shortened the exposed Dutch coastline by two-thirds,
L148@P6: • the Maeslant Barrier, two large swinging gates—each the size of the Eiffel
L149@P6: Tower—completed in 1997 to protect Rotterdam, its port and surrounding areas
L150@P6: These structures combine to provide the Netherlands with a very high level of
L151@P6: flood protection. Areas that are most vulnerable to flooding with a high economic and human value have flood protection infrastructure designed to withstand
L152@P6: a 1 in 10,000 year flood. The Netherlands, however, is continually refining and
L153@P6: updating flood protection policy, most recently by incorporating risk management concepts into that policy. This new practice moves away from designing
L154@P6: infrastructure to withstand a theoretical storm and toward designing, inspecting
L155@P6: and maintaining flood protection to reduce the actual probability of flooding in
L156@P6: any and all areas. The policy also helps officials set priorities and make more
L157@P6: informed decisions about where to invest resources in any given year.
L158@P6-7: For more information, see www.deltawerken.nl/english.13

L160@P7: Water Management Expertise
L161@P7: Dutch expertise with water is not limited to flood control. It extends to several
L162@P7: areas of water management, particularly the ones mentioned below.
L163@P7: Integrated Water Management
L164@P7: • Integrated water management: water governance and sustainable use of
L165@P7: water resources
L166@P7: • Partnerships: building national and international partnerships and water
L167@P7: networks
L168@P7: • Institutional development: institutional capacity building (administrative,
L169@P7: legislative, and managerial), training and education, knowledge exchange
L170@P7: Delta Technology
L171@P7: • Water management: monitoring of groundwater and surface water, irrigation,
L172@P7: drainage, drinking water supply and sanitation
L173@P7: • Flood protection/management of flood risks
L174@P7: • Hydraulic engineering: dredging; land reclamation, port, dike, and dam
L175@P7: construction, maintenance of soft sandy coasts
L176@P7: • Spatial planning using water as a guiding principle for spatial development:
L177@P7: multifunctional land use in densely populated areas, combined urban development and water storage, the development of nature reserves and recreational
L178@P7: areas, coastal zones and estuaries
L179@P7: • Environmental conservation: ecological restoration of rivers and coastal zones,
L180@P7: wetland management, protection of biodiversity and waterfowl
L181@P7: habitats, and the wise use of wetlands, mangroves, and coral reefs
L182@P7: Water Technology
L183@P7: • Water supply for domestic and industrial uses: the Netherlands’ public drinking
L184@P7: water supplies reach almost 100 percent of the population, providing water
L185@P7: of the highest quality without the use of disinfectants or chlorination. Many
L186@P7: industries can use recycled water where quality is adjusted to meet the needs
L187@P7: of key production processes
L188@P7: • Wastewater treatment and sanitation

L197@P8: ROYAL NETHERLANDS EMBASSY PIONEERING WATER
L198@P8: Dutch history can be marked by repeated, and often overwhelming, floods. The
L199@P8: aftermath of each flood saw a strengthening of flood defenses and improvements
L200@P8: to supporting infrastructure. Indeed, the overall level of protection from flooding
L201@P8: in the Netherlands is quite high. The highest level of protection—provided to
L202@P8: cities and areas with a high-density of human and economic capital—in the
L203@P8: Netherlands is designed to withstand a 1 in 10,000 year flood. The lowest
L204@P8: level of protection—designed for inland, rural and sparsely populated areas
L205@P8: —is designed to withstand a 1 in 1,250 year flood.
L206@P8: In recent years Dutch officials have begun to incorporate risk management
L207@P8: concepts into flood policy. By doing so, the Dutch government is able to protect
L208@P8: its citizens more effectively and efficiently. One aspect of risk management
L209@P8: is the division of the land into dike ring compartments that have different risk
L210@P8: levels of flooding. Another change has been to move away from designing infrastructure to withstand a theoretical storm and toward designing, inspecting and
L211@P8: maintaining flood protection to reduce the actual probability of flooding in any
L212@P8: and all areas. Good data provided by routine, mandatory inspections is crucial
L213@P8: to this change. Risk management concepts also help establish priorities in any
L214@P8: given year by targeting resources on the weakest links in the chain.
L215@P8: Good risk management also requires evolving best practices. Good water management is not a static process. Dutch water management policy constantly
L216@P8: adapts to domestic, international, and atmospheric developments. For example,
L217@P8: new procedures enable Dutch officials to better understand the cost-benefit
L218@P8: aspects of flood protection decisions. The Dutch national government, provincial
L219@P8: governments, and local water boards will jointly implement the new “Safe
L220@P8: Netherlands Roadmap,” which requires:
L221@P8: Risk Management in the
L222@P8: Twenty-first Century
L223@P8-9: What Protection At What Cost?16 17
L224@P9: ROYAL NETHERLANDS EMBASSY PIONEERING WATER • mandatory inspections of all flood protection infrastructure no less than once
L225@P9: every five years
L226@P9: • assessments of all possible failure mechanisms—whether caused by natural
L227@P9: or human factors of the infrastructure—in the dike ring compartments
L228@P9: • calculations of the probability of flooding should failure occur • GIS technology, demographic and insurance damage “curves” that help predict
L229@P9: potential flood damage, both human and economic, from particular failures, and
L230@P9: • rigorous cost-benefit analyses that crystallize policy alternatives, guide decisions,
L231@P9: and explain to the public the rationale behind decisions
L232@P9: Successful risk management begins with communicating to the public and
L233@P9: key stakeholders what the well-defined, acceptable levels of risk are. Broadly
L234@P9: speaking, acceptable risk is the scientifically established probability of loss
L235@P9: of life and economic damage that will result from the failure of an engineered
L236@P9: system, such as dams, levees, gates, weirs, or the water system’s ability to
L237@P9: temporarily absorb or divert excess water. “How safe is safe?” and “How much
L238@P9: money will a specific level of safety cost?” are important engineering and policy
L239@P9: questions that guide acceptable risk determinations. In order to improve risk
L240@P9: assessment practices and to refine levels of acceptable risk, the Dutch collabo-
L241@P9: rate with their counterparts in countries around the world, including the United
L242@P9: States, where they consult with experts in the Army Corps of Engineers, the
L243@P9: Bureau of Reclamation, and in many state governments.

L247@P10: ROYAL NETHERLANDS EMBASSY PIONEERING WATER
L248@P10: In May 2004, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and the Dutch
L249@P10: Rijkswaterstaat (RWS) signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) to collaborate
L250@P10: on policy and water resources planning and management. The Rijkswaterstaat is
L251@P10: part of the Netherlands Ministry of Transport, Public Works and Water Management
L252@P10: and is responsible for flood prevention and for the main road, water transport and
L253@P10: traffic arteries. USACE is a counterpart of RWS in the United States in the field
L254@P10: of water management.
L255@P10: Within the MOA, USACE and RWS have held recurring technical workshops on a
L256@P10: variety of themes including water management, levees, evacuation, and damage
L257@P10: mitigation. The MOA also facilitates many other activities. At the corporate level,
L258@P10: a joint study is comparing and contrasting the water management history of both
L259@P10: countries. At a strategic level, high-level management and top specialists from
L260@P10: USACE and RWS regularly exchange and participate in each other’s councils,
L261@P10: conferences, and working groups.
L262@P10: The aftermath of Hurricanes Rita and Katrina has given particular focus and
L263@P10: vitality to this partnership. Both parties are using the lessons that disasters
L264@P10: of this magnitude teach to learn from one another on issues related to coastal
L265@P10: zone protection and management. Their cooperative efforts began with the
L266@P10: New Orleans area, but they have grown to include the area around Sacramento,
L267@P10: California as well. Moreover, discussions are underway to determine whether
L268@P10: cooperation with Florida would be fruitful.

L282@P12: New Orleans The lower Mississippi River Delta and the lower Rhine River Delta in the
L283@P12: Netherlands are quite alike. Both deltas drain large parts of their respective
L284@P12: continents; both are key locations for commerce, shipping, fishing, and other
L285@P12: economic activity; both serve as hubs for nearby oil and gas development; and
L286@P12: both are beautiful, ecologically rich and environmentally sensitive areas. Both
L287@P12: areas, moreover, are home to culturally rich communities that lie below sea
L288@P12: level and are vulnerable to periodic, often catastrophic, flooding.
L289@P12: Katrina Response
L290@P12: Within hours after Hurricane Katrina made landfall, the Dutch government
L291@P12: dispatched mobile pumps, civil engineers, and a Royal Navy frigate, a quick
L292@P12: response made possible by the Memorandum of Agreement between the
L293@P12: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the Dutch Rijkswaterstaat.
L294@P12: Post-Katrina, the Memorandum has enabled further interaction between the
L295@P12: Corps and Dutch experts in New Orleans and the surrounding area, including:
L296@P12: • inspection of the federal Hurricane Protection System levees protecting New
L297@P12: Orleans by the Dutch firms Arcadis, Fugro, Haskoning, and DHV
L298@P12: • geotechnical analysis of subsoils and hydromorphic conditions along the
L299@P12: lower Mississippi river by Fugro, DHV, and Haskoning
L300@P12: • design assistance on emergency repairs to damaged levees and flood control
L301@P12: structures by Arcadis and Haskoning
L302@P12: • conceptual studies for two large storm surge barriers to protect New Orleans
L303@P12: by Arcadis and WL Delft Hydraulics, and
L304@P12: • a Dutch perspective on the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration plan
L305@P12: Dutch government, academic, and private sector experts are also in close contact
L306@P12: with officials from the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development,
L307@P12: the Louisiana Department of Natural Resources, the Louisiana Coastal Protection
L308@P12: and Restoration Authority, and the New Orleans City Council.

L316@P13: Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration (LACPR)
L317@P13: In late 2005, the U.S. Congress mandated that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
L318@P13: submit to Congress a detailed, long-term plan to provide protection for New Orleans
L319@P13: against a Category 5 hurricane. This protection would be over and above the
L320@P13: already existing, but not yet fulfilled, requirement for the Corps to provide 1 in
L321@P13: 100 year storm protection for New Orleans.
L322@P13: The Corps has engaged a team of Netherlands Water Partnership members—
L323@P13: including the Rijkswaterstaat, Arcadis, Fugro, DHV, Infram, WL Delft Hydraulics,
L324@P13: HKV and Haskoning—to deliver a conceptual study of how Dutch engineers
L325@P13: would provide Category 5 protection for New Orleans. The Dutch team and
L326@P13: various members of the Corps have held numerous interactive workshops,
L327@P13: and both Corps and Dutch officials praise this interaction for deepening the
L328@P13: understanding of challenges in New Orleans and the costs/benefits of various
L329@P13: policy alternatives. The study—tentatively entitled “The Dutch Perspective on
L330@P13: Louisiana Coastal Restoration and Protection”—will be included as an appendix
L331@P13: to the Corps’ submission to Congress.
L332@P13: Spatial Planning
L333@P13: Protecting New Orleans from future flood disasters will require stronger, armored
L334@P13: levees, restored coastal wetlands, and effective pump stations. Creating a safe
L335@P13: and revitalized New Orleans means also incorporating concepts of safety, risk
L336@P13: mitigation, and flood protection redundancy into public infrastructure and urban
L337@P13: and economic redevelopment plans.
L338@P13: This is also being done in the Netherlands, where provincial and local governments
L339@P13: and project developers must provide a water safety plan for every residential,
L340@P13: commercial, industrial, and agricultural development project. Local water
L341@P13: boards, public safety officials, city planners, landscape architects and project
L342@P13: developers collaborate to ensure that all new development is integrated into,
L343@P13: and does not subtract from, current flood protection levels.
L344@P13: In practice, this means that infrastructure additions—roads, rail, bridges, culverts,
L345@P13: sewers, and even public transit stations—should enhance water diversion, storage
L346@P13: and absorption capacities and provide redundancy to existing flood protection
L347@P13: structures. Landscape architects can design, and even redesign, a development’s “water footprint,” mitigating its impact on local flood protection while
L348@P13: enhancing aesthetic and economic values. Civil architects and developers
L349@P13: can create safe residential communities where access to water is a key selling
L350@P13: point. Safety, recreation, mixed land use and environmental goals can be mutually
L351@P13: reinforcing when one adopts a Live-with-the-Water approach.
L352@P13: The American Planning Association, the New Orleans City Council, and the New
L353@P13: Orleans Redevelopment Authority have turned to Dutch landscape architects,
L354@P13: civil engineers, the Netherlands Institute for Housing and Spatial Planning, and
L355@P13: Dutch government officials for advice and assistance on post-Katrina rebuilding
L356@P13: and redevelopment.
L357@P13: Storm Surge Barriers
L358@P13: Pursuant to a request from the US Army Corps of Engineers in New Orleans,
L359@P13: WL Delft Hydraulics—a leading technical research and consulting institute
L360@P13: based in the Netherlands—and Arcadis—a large Dutch-American engineering
L361@P13: firm—provided a conceptual design study explaining how two moveable storm
L362@P13: surge barriers in New Orleans’ Inner Navigation Canal and the Gulf Intracoastal
L363@P13: Waterway could be used to substantially decrease storm surge and wave levels
L364@P13-14: in and around New Orleans.26 27
L365@P14: ROYAL NETHERLANDS EMBASSY PIONEERING WATER
L366@P14: Emergency Planning
L367@P14: and Disaster Response
L368@P14: Are Katrina’s Lessons and the United States’
L369@P14: Experiences Relevant to Europe?
L370@P14: Hurricane Katrina was the United States’ worst natural disaster. It overwhelmed
L371@P14: protective infrastructure and exposed weaknesses in existing emergency response
L372@P14: and disaster preparedness procedures. Many people in the Netherlands have
L373@P14: asked how Dutch preparedness measures would perform during and after a
L374@P14: storm like Katrina. After considering this question and observing Katrina’s impact,
L375@P14: the Netherlands’ overwhelming focus on disaster prevention has evolved to also
L376@P14: include more robust disaster response, evacuation and communications techniques
L377@P14: to mitigate the harmful consequences of a disaster. In short, Katrina convinced
L378@P14: the Dutch that planning primarily to prevent a disaster was no longer sufficient,
L379@P14: and that planning for the aftermath of a disaster would also be required. Katrina
L380@P14: has had a similar effect on emergency planning in other European capitals.
L381@P14: As part of its cooperative efforts with the United States, Dutch government
L382@P14: officials and disaster response experts have asked their peers in Louisiana,
L383@P14: California, and Washington, DC, the following questions:
L384@P14: 1. What lessons might Europeans extract from the actual experience the United
L385@P14: States has in planning, preparing, responding, and recovering from these kinds
L386@P14: of super-storms?
L387@P14: 2. Does European remote sensing, earth observation, early warning, and public
L388@P14: broadcasting technology hold any benefits for the United States and the
L389@P14: international community-at-large?
L390@P14: 3. What is the current state of, and what are the future perspectives on, transatlantic cooperation in crisis management?
L391@P14: 4. Would perhaps a ‘merger’ of U.S. and European knowledge and experience in
L392@P14: crisis management be beneficial to other low-lying parts of the world?
L393@P14: Joint cooperation and the sharing of best practices in this area will pay huge
L394@P14: dividends. Some projects underway include:
L395@P14: • The International Katrina Book (IKB) project seeks to mobilize focused feedback
L396@P14: from different countries, professions, disciplines, and the private and public
